In January 1952 , Headlam was appointed WingCommander ( WgCdr ) of No. 229 OCU , RAF Coningsby . Promoted to group captain in January 1954 , he became Station Commander at RAF Syerston . In January 1956 , Headlam was appointed Air Attaché to the United States . He returned to the UK in December 1958 , when he became Commandant of the Central Flying School , RAF Little Rissington . Promoted to air vice marshal ( AVM ) in April 1963 , Headlam became Deputy Chief Scientific Advisor at the Ministry of Defence . Following a year's sick leave , he took over as Chief Inspector of the Royal Air Force in February 1965 . He retired in July 1968 .

## High Commissioner of British Guiana

Headlam was appointed High Commissioner of British Guiana from 1960 to 1961 . The position was a high-profile one amidst intense international scrutiny given the country's longstanding desire for independence, its strong economy and its strategic location on the northeastern coast of South America. The country had a history of political turbulence and racial strife as well as widespread suspicion of British imperialism. Headlam was knighted on 11 June 1961 . He was appointed a Priv

Department of Civil Aviation , then was seconded in 1946 to the British Overseas Airways Corporation (BOAC) to assist with its postwar expansion. In 1947 he was appointed BOAC's Director of Flying Operations, responsible for introducing BOAC's first pressurised-cabin airliners, the Canadair North Star, the piston-engined Douglas DC-6B and de Havilland Comet jet.

In 1955 Headlam became Senior Vice-President of BOAC, a position he held until his retirement in 1965. That year, he was appointed a Knight Commander of the Order of the British Empire.

## Personal life and death

Headlam married Barbara Margaret Jackson in 1942 in Bermuda . They had two children, a daughter and a son. Headlam died by suicide in 1977. He shot himself in the head while driving his car, at home near Maidenhead .

It has a picturesque town centre with beautiful views, as well as having a very vibrant atmosphere with lots to see and do. We would recommend a visit to the medieval Tudor house to see a glimpse of this bygone Tudor world and how those from that era would have lived.

We would also recommend a visit to the St Mary Redcliffe’s church which is one of the city most impressive medieval buildings as well as having some excellent views from its bell tower. It is also worth taking a trip to the Museum of Bristol which is home to some of the most important artefacts of the cities past.

If you prefer the outdoors type, the nearby Cheddar Gorge with its incredible caves, stunning limestone cliffs and dramatic underground river, is well worth a visit.

Meridian boasts several restaurants, cafés and bars where you can choose from a range of local cuisines and refreshments.

## Early life[edit | edit source]

Chak Tok Ich 'aak I acceded to the throne at a young age in AD 292. His father was Yax Ehb Xook, the twelfth ruler of Tikal and his mother was Lady Une' B'alam. He only reigned for three years before a succession dispute erupted, possibly as a result of his young age (his father was still alive). One of his uncles, Siyaj Chan K'awiil, challenged him for the throne. This led to the accession of his uncle, who was given the title of Ah Siyaj, which means "Watery Sky", as well as the numeral 'ajaw-'ok numberals.

A dynastic chronology is well established for much of the Classic Period; seven rulers are known between the earliest date, which carries a Calendar Round (CR) date corresponding to 13 September 330, and the latest, which corresponds to 14 September 605. The last date that can be positively related to one of the city's known rulers is 14 August 680.
